title: Macros Explained in 30 Seconds #shorts
description:
Everything you eat is just 3 things: carbs, protein and fat. Carbs and protein have 4 calories per gram. Fat has 9.

Calories decide your weight. Macros decide what that weight is made of.

Part 1 of 20 in the FORM THEORY Nutrition 101 series: nutrition made simple for beginners.

title: What Are Carbs, Really? #shorts
description:
Carbs are your body's main fuel: sugars, starches and fiber, digested into glucose for energy. Extra carbs are stored as glycogen in your muscles and liver, ready for your next workout.

title: Cutting Carbs? Watch This First #shorts
description:
Carbs fuel hard training, your brain runs mainly on glucose, they refill muscle glycogen and fiber keeps digestion healthy. Low-carb can work for fat loss, but total calories decide fat loss, not carbs alone.

title: Simple vs Complex Carbs (When to Eat Each) #shorts
description:
Simple carbs digest fast for quick energy: fruit, honey, juice. Complex carbs digest slowly for steady energy: oats, rice, potatoes, beans. Use simple carbs around training and complex carbs for most meals.

title: Fiber: The Carb Most People Miss #shorts
description:
Aim for about 25 g of fiber a day for women and 38 g for men. Most people eat far less. Fiber keeps you full longer, helps digestion and steadies blood sugar. Easy sources: chia seeds, oats, lentils, fruit.

title: Protein Isn't Just for Bodybuilders #shorts
description:
Protein is your body's building blocks: amino acids that build muscle, skin, hormones and enzymes. 9 of them are essential, meaning your body can't make them and they must come from food. Protein has 4 calories per gram.

title: 4 Reasons to Eat More Protein #shorts
description:
Protein builds and repairs muscle, keeps you full longer, burns more calories to digest (about 20-30% of its calories vs 5-10% for carbs and 0-3% for fat) and protects muscle while you diet.

title: How Much Protein Do You Actually Need? #shorts
description:
If you don't exercise: about 0.8 g per kg of body weight. If you train: 1.4-2.0 g per kg (International Society of Sports Nutrition). Example: 70 kg = 98-140 g a day. Split it over 3-4 meals of about 20-40 g.

title: Fat Doesn't Make You Fat #shorts
description:
Eating too many calories does. Fat is the most energy-dense macro at 9 calories per gram. Unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish): eat more. Saturated (butter, ghee, cheese): some. Trans fats: avoid.

title: Cutting All Fat Is a Bad Idea #shorts
description:
Fat helps make hormones including testosterone, lets you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, provides essential omega-3 and omega-6, and makes meals satisfying. Aim for about 20-35% of your calories from fat.

title: Good Fat vs Bad Fat #shorts
description:
Eat more: olive oil, nuts and seeds, fatty fish, avocado. Limit: deep-fried food, pastries and biscuits, processed meat, lots of butter. Avoid trans fats: check labels for "partially hydrogenated oil".

title: What Is a Calorie? #shorts
description:
A calorie is a unit of energy. Food gives it, your body burns it to stay alive and move. Count any meal: grams of carbs x 4 + grams of protein x 4 + grams of fat x 9. Example: 40 g carbs, 30 g protein, 15 g fat = 415 kcal.

title: What Are Maintenance Calories? #shorts
description:
Your maintenance calories are what keeps your weight the same. Typically most of it (around 65%) keeps you alive (BMR), around 25% goes to movement and exercise, and around 10% to digesting food. Varies by person.

title: Calculate Your BMR in 30 Seconds #shorts
description:
Mifflin-St Jeor formula: 10 x weight (kg) + 6.25 x height (cm) - 5 x age, then +5 for men or -161 for women. Example: man, 25, 75 kg, 175 cm = about 1,724 kcal.

title: How to Calculate Your Maintenance Calories #shorts
description:
Multiply your BMR by your activity factor: 1.2 sedentary, 1.375 light (1-3 days/week), 1.55 moderate (3-5 days), 1.725 very active (6-7 days). Example: 1,724 x 1.55 = about 2,672 kcal. It's an estimate: track your weight for 2 weeks and adjust by 100-200 kcal.

title: Fat Loss in One Sentence #shorts
description:
Burn more than you eat. Your body covers the gap mostly with stored fat. Example: burn 2,672 kcal, eat 2,172 kcal, and a 500 kcal daily gap comes mostly from body fat.

title: How Big Should Your Calorie Deficit Be? #shorts
description:
Start with about 500 kcal a day below maintenance. 500 x 7 days = 3,500 kcal, roughly 0.5 kg of fat a week. Aim to lose 0.5-1% of your body weight per week, go slower if you're losing muscle, and recalculate as you lose weight.
